issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Arthur, at sixty years old, presented with a quiet weariness that seemed to settle deep in his bones, a stark contrast to the robust frame one might expect of a man who spent decades as a warehouse worker. He sought help on the urging of his partner, admitting that the invisible weight he carried from his military service had become unbearable, particularly in recent years.

Decades ago, Arthur had been deployed to a dense, humid jungle environment. The traumatic event that haunted him involved an ambush during a patrol, a chaotic explosion of sound and violence. He remembered the deafening crack of gunfire, the screams of his comrades, and the sickening smell of burning foliage. Separated from his unit in the confusion, he had hidden, terrified, as the sounds of battle raged around him, eventually emerging to find many of his friends gone. When Arthur forced himself to recall the horror of that day, the terror on recall was as visceral as if it were happening again, and with it came an intense guilt on recall, a crushing weight for having survived when others did not. This constant internal replay of the ambush, witnessing his comrades fall while he survived, solidified his overwhelming sense of survival guilt, making him believe he was somehow undeserving of life and that the world is a dangerous place.

Because Arthur was tormented by this pervasive survival guilt and the conviction that the world is a dangerous place, he began to instinctively avoid thinking about the event entirely, pushing it down, burying it. He reasoned that if he didn't dwell on the past, he could protect himself from further pain and perhaps even from the perceived dangers lurking everywhere. This protective instinct also led him to avoid wearing similar clothes to his old uniform, opting for civilian attire that offered no hint of his military past, as they were a stark reminder of the dangerous world he had once inhabited and the guilt he carried. Over the years, Arthur’s determined efforts to avoid thinking about the traumatic event, pushing away any memory of his military service, gradually led to a profound sense of identity loss. He felt disconnected from the young man he once was, wondering who he even was without that defining, yet unspoken, chapter of his life, further deepening his internal struggle and sense of alienation.

His deeply held conviction that the world is a dangerous place, a belief forged in the crucible of combat, colored every attempt at remembering. When a memory did surface, it was immediately filtered through this lens, amplifying the terror on recall and the guilt on recall, making the past feel not just painful, but actively threatening, as if re-experiencing it would confirm his worst fears about the pervasive danger. Even when he wasn't actively trying to recall, sudden sensory cues at his warehouse job—the metallic clang of a dropped pallet echoing like gunfire, the humid air of a storage unit feeling like the jungle—would trigger an immediate terror on recall, plunging him back into the ambush. In response, Arthur would immediately avoid the location in the warehouse, sometimes taking circuitous routes through the aisles or finding excuses to be elsewhere, anything to escape the visceral flashback and the accompanying dread. This pattern of avoidance, developed over decades, had become an ingrained habit.

He found that even when he tried to speak about his past with his partner, the words simply wouldn't come, a frustrating blankness taking hold as he struggled to articulate the inexpressible horror.

The cumulative effect of these internal battles had begun to strain his relationship. His partner often felt shut out, unable to understand the invisible wall Arthur had built around himself. He was tired, perpetually on edge, and the constant mental effort to avoid thinking about the past left him drained. Arthur finally sought help because he was tired of feeling like a stranger to himself, trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, yearning to understand why the world still felt so dangerous and why he carried such profound guilt for simply surviving.
